extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in constitutional design and representative government
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical recommendations for composing legislatures, structuring the executive, and appointing officials in representative governments. Emphasizes checks on majority rule, responsibility in administration, and the qualifications and selection of second chambers, ministers, civil servants, and judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of a Second Chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: A Second Chamber is of comparatively little importance if other constitutional questions are rightly decided; it offers checks only where the democratic principle is otherwise unchecked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author sets little value on any check a Second Chamber can apply to an otherwise unchecked democracy, and thinks the importance of having two Chambers versus one is comparatively small when other constitutional arrangements are sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Similar Composition of Two Chambers
rubrics_metrics.description: If both chambers are similarly composed they will obey the same influences and majorities will likely coincide, making the second chamber a poor additional check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While requiring consent of both houses can delay measures (a small minority might block), this delay is often temporary and may prompt a fresh appeal to electors; the inconvenience of delay and the value of appeal to the nation can balance out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Chamber as a School of Conciliation
rubrics_metrics.description: A second chamber can promote conciliation, compromise, and moderation by preventing the corrupting effect of undivided power and reminding holders of power of others' perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mutual give-and-take between two houses fosters readiness to concede and shape measures less offensively to opponents; this habit is a perpetual school useful especially in more democratic constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy of Second Chamber Depends on External Social Support
rubrics_metrics.description: A chamber intended to check democracy is only effective if it commands social support outside the House; an aristocratic House is powerful only in an aristocratic society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the social force behind a second chamber is weak relative to the democratic majority, it cannot act as an effective check and must operate by allying with elements in the crowd rather than confronting it openly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderating Power Must Operate Through the Democratic House
rubrics_metrics.description: The real moderating force in a democratic constitution should act in and through the democratic House rather than in bitter opposition to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A second chamber should not appear as an antagonist provoking a rally against it, but work as one element among many, infusing influence to shape outcomes without provoking general resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a Centre of Resistance to Majority Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Every polity should have a centre of resistance to the predominant power; in democracies a nucleus of resistance to the democracy is a fundamental maxim of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This centre can take various shapes depending on historical antecedents; tolerance for a second chamber is a reason for having it, but it is not the only or best shape intrinsically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Chamber Should Represent Personal Merit and Experience
rubrics_metrics.description: If one house represents popular feeling, the other should represent personal merit, tested by public service and fortified by practical experience (a Chamber of Statesmen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested composition includes former members of a legislative commission, chief justices or heads of superior courts, judges with five years' service, former cabinet ministers with two years' service, commanders-in-chief, governors-general, long-serving colonial governors, and senior permanent civil servants; scientific and literary eminence are excluded as too disputable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Eligibility to Prevent Party Jobbing
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualifications for a senatorial dignity should be tied to legal, political, military, or naval functions and limited by time in office to prevent naming ministers merely to give them seats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time conditions (e.g., two years for cabinet office) prevent appointments for the purpose of senatorial seats and align eligibility with demonstrated service and pension qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting Hereditary Peerage Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where hereditary peerage persists, peers might be present by representatives chosen among themselves rather than personally, to avoid exclusive representation by the largest party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes grouping peers (e.g., one representative per ten peers), peer voting procedures including nomination, proxy voting, threshold (ten votes), and lotteries to form constituencies so representation is more proportional and less monopolized by a single party in the peerage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Chamber Elected by the First as an Acceptable Alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: A Second Chamber elected by the First (but not selecting its own members) could be acceptable: it would be popular-choice once removed and unlikely to clash with the popular House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided minority representation is secured, such a chamber would probably be well composed and include capable men who might not seek popular election themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Should Avoid Class Interests and Be Acceptable to Democratic Feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The best constitution of a Second Chamber embodies many elements exempt from class interests while being unoffensive to democratic sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chamber should not be a class-opposed body; its task is to temper majority ascendancy without incurring hostility by being seen as an unfair privileged class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departments Should Correspond to Subjects (Single Authority for Single Ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of executive functionaries should correspond to the classification of subjects; where the object to be attained is single, authority should be single and responsibility unified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid multiple independent departments supervising parts of the same natural whole, because divided authorities prioritize their own means and sacrifice the real end; e.g., military administration should be unified under one control for efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear Individual Responsibility for Executive Functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every executive function should be the appointed duty of a given individual so it is apparent who did everything and who is responsible for omissions or errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility is null when nobody knows who is responsible; concentration of praise and blame on one person maintains accountability. Division can enfeeble or destroy responsibility, especially when acts are those of a majority (boards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Boards for Executive Business When Possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards are generally unfit for executive business because collective decision-making conceals individual responsibility; 'boards are screens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards may be admissible when giving full discretionary power to a single minister would be worse, but otherwise executive acts should be attributable to identifiable individuals supported by advisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide Ministers with Permanent, Responsible Advisers and Councils
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers, especially in specialized departments (e.g., military, naval), should have councils of able, experienced professional men who are permanent and whose recorded opinions make clear what advice was given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Councils should be consultative; ultimate decision rests with the minister, but advisers must be placed under conditions making it impossible to avoid expressing opinions and making the minister listen; recording differing views increases transparency and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional Permanent Civil Service and Fixed-Term High Appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: A permanent professional civil service should supply the councils and advisers; high appointments reached by selection (not promotion) should be for fixed terms unless reappointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed terms reduce jobbing, allow removal without affront, and enable bringing in younger qualified persons; abolition of professional civil service or councils would weaken effective administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive and Other Skilled Offices Should Not Be Filled by Popular Election
rubrics_metrics.description: No executive functionaries should be appointed by popular election (neither by the people nor their representatives) because government is skilled employment requiring professional judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting the fittest persons requires laborious, conscientious discernment and knowledge of candidates—tasks ill-suited to popular voting; ministers should be accountable for subordinate selections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Parliamentary Appointment of Chief Executive over Popular Election
rubrics_metrics.description: In republics, the chief magistrate is better appointed by the representative body than chosen by popular election, which tends to yield obscure or non-political candidates and produces continuous electioneering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointment by Parliament produces more eminent leaders, avoids perpetual canvassing that reduces public affairs to personal party struggles, and alternatives include appointment for a fixed period with dissolution powers to balance independence and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Should Have Power to Dissolve Parliament to Avoid Deadlocks
rubrics_metrics.description: The head of the administration ought to have the power to dissolve the House and appeal to the people so that deadlocks between executive and assembly can be resolved constitutionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissolution prevents prolonged paralysis where neither side can legally remove the other, provides a constitutional means of testing contested party strength, and prevents interregnums that stall public business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where Coup Risk Exists the Executive Must Be Removable by Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: In states where vast power is centralized and attachment to free institutions is weak, no first magistrate is admissible whom Parliament cannot by a single vote reduce to private station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the risk of subversion is real, ensuring the executive's constitutional dependence on Parliament is essential to prevent usurpation of sovereign power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Appointments Should Avoid Popular Election and Preserve Judicial Independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial officers should not be appointed by popular election because their professional qualifications are least fit for popular judgment and impartiality is paramount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While irremovability has evils (difficulty removing bad judges), responsibility to popular vote or government risks perverting judicial conduct; removal mechanisms should be carefully designed to balance independence and accountability.
